en: By the phrase "having subdued the flesh-eater at the time of death," it is indicated that, just as with Makaranda, Madhava’s fulfillment of his affection through gratitude is shown by his protection of Malati. Thus, when the entry of Aghoraghanta and Kapalakundala is indicated, and Madhava’s entry into the cremation ground occurs via his vow to sell human flesh, the commencement of the Act (ankarambha) takes place. (1)

[KAPĀLAKUṆḌALĀ] [1] "Exceeding the six" means: among the wheels (*cakras*)—which are like wheels because of the sequential movement of the specific vital breath (*prāṇa*) presided over by a single cause through the junctions of the channels (*nāḍī*) at the six locations of the union of Śiva and Śakti, namely the root, the navel, the heart, the throat, the palate, and the space between the eyebrows—that which is "exceeding," i.e., the primary one, is the wheel of ten channels; its center is the heart.

In that wheel—characterized by the ten channels (nāḍīs), namely iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā, gāndhārī, hastijihvā, pūṣā, yaśasvinī, lambuṣā, kuhū, and śaṅkhinī, which are the most prominent among the one hundred and one channels located within the heart and extending transversely, upwards, and downwards—the Self resides. It is situated in the center of the lotus, within the subtle space of the covered region, at the site of the great churning-stick (manthāna) of the body, which consists of the union of both prāṇa and apāna. The Self [resides] there.

Knowledge is the nature of pure, immutably established, and unobscured consciousness; he who possesses that [knowledge] is victorious—this is the grammatical connection. (2) Although it remains pervading the body from head to foot, nevertheless its supreme abode is the casket of the heart-lotus.

According to this statement, "staying there" means the manifestation of the reality of the Supreme Self—which is filled with the majesty of qualities such as omniscience, consisting of the light of unobscured consciousness that is a mass of the bliss of pure awareness, and free from all conceptual constructions—within the mental application directed toward that [Self]. (3) "Having his form placed in the heart": when meditated upon, he bestows the attainment of all desired fruits. Is this so for everyone? No; he says it is for "those who know that. "Tāḥ" refers to...

(3) *Siddhiḥ*: for those who attain [it] by means of the proper method, place, time, measure, instrument, and procedure. (4) *Avicalitam*: by those practitioners whose minds have become motionless—that is to say, withdrawn from other objects—[and are thus] of such a nature.

By the word "being sought" (*mṛgyamāṇa*), it is stated that although [the reality] is unobscured in that place, it does not immediately become an object of capable direct perception for them due to the knot of the innate grasping of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) toward the body and other objects; therefore, it is not rejected merely because of the non-perception of something suitable.

Likewise, he is "bound" (*naddha*)—meaning surrounded—on all sides by the eight presiding deities known as Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍikā, who are designated by the term *puryaṣṭaka*, and by their powers consisting of knowledge, will, action, and so forth; yet he is not made dependent by them, but rather is their "Lord" (*nātha*), the cause for the manifestation of their sovereignty, as it has been said: "We praise Śaṅkara, the source of the glory of the wheel of powers.
(5) For this very reason, it is said that he "is victorious"—that is, he exists as the sovereign over all activity and cessation. [1]

[2] Thus, having performed prostration to the Blessed One—who manifests the distinction between the higher and the lower within a mind perfumed by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the supreme reality—the author, desiring to explain within his own self the power of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) on the non-difference between the supreme and the individual soul (*jīva*) as revealed by such instructions as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), says: "Always placed," and so forth. Those six wheels (*cakras*) which were previously mentioned in relation to the "limbs"—that is, the body—which are to be brought into proximity through the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and the activity of the person, and which are always present due to their distinct locations in the heart, head, crest-lock (*śikhā*), and so on;

Although their heart-lotus had been obscured by the onset of the activity of the possession of the demon of sense-objects—manifested through the arousal of various individualizing factors that act as life-breaths for obstacles to manifold awakening—they beheld the Self in the form of Śiva, manifested within the middle of the *dahara*-space situated at the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus, and have thus arrived at this place.

(6) If the Self is manifested there in that manner, why does it not appear clearly to everyone? To this, he states the cause for its clear manifestation: "by virtue of absorption" (*layavaśāt*). This is because of the cessation of all fluctuations of the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), attained in the state where the mind has been brought under control through the practice of conquering the winds [of the body]. As it is said: "Where the vital breaths and the mind are naturally restrained, there you are seen by those free from all defects, and not by others."

(7) Likewise, regarding the emergence (*udaya*) of the channels (*nāḍī*), beginning with *iḍā*—which is the manifestation of the wheel of rays such as the sovereign power of the left (*vāmeśvaryādi*) inherent within them—by means of that sequence, according to the order of their arising, there are five "nectars" (*amṛta*) belonging to the world consisting of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) such as earth. These consist of essence-power (*sāra-śakti*), are characterized by sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, are imperishable, and nourish the subtle measures (*mātrā*) of the gross elements. Through the enjoyment of these by the Yoginīs, the cage of the elements (*bhūtapañjara*) [of beings] such as humans becomes like a scale-plate (*śalka*).

By tasting that essence, through supreme repose, the yoginīs attain a certain power, a certain majesty, unsurpassed good fortune, and the manifestation of divine knowledge; thus, by drawing forth those five nectars according to the principle of extracting and accepting sugarcane juice and so forth, they dispel the clouds standing before them—those in front of them—without experiencing the exhaustion of ascending to the heights of the sky, solely due to the extraordinary power manifested by their own majesty.
Dividing [the clouds] into two. (8) If the reading is *nabhaḥ*, however, the meaning is "shattering the clouds in the sky.

[2] [3] Regarding *udvṛttā* ("upturned"): the speed of her journey through the expanse of the sky brings about a complete connection between my state of loveliness and her own intensity. By the force of that speed, the necklace of skulls made of cranial fragments moves upward and then falters. Then, due to the clashing of the mass of skulls gathered from the distant fall, the tiny bells ring out—*karālam* meaning "unevenly" or "harshly.
[3] To the question, "In what way is there both loveliness and ferocity? he says, "For thus... (*tathā hi*).

[4] Even the mass of matted hair (*jaṭā*), though bound with tight knots, spreads out and quivers in every direction. There exists a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that persists for a long time through its own nature within the sound previously produced; mixed with that, there arises a fresh and ever-new resonance. By means of this, the bell—attached to a wooden staff held by a human skull-cup and bound with a garland, having been whirled in a circle for as long as possible—resounds. Through its clarity, it produces a state of loveliness; it brings about immortality (*āmara-tva*).

The wind shakes the banner aloft. As for the "openings": those hollow cavities of the fleshless, dried-out heads of corpses; the "rows" are the lines of these [heads]; their "bowers" are the dense, secluded spots; resounding within those bowers—and for this very reason, "tumultuous," meaning formidable—the wind becomes the cause of the tinkling sound produced by the movement of the small bells. [4]

When garlic (*rasona*) that has been sprinkled with oil from the *purāṇanimba* tree is being roasted, a foul odor arises due to its placement in the midst of the fire; such is the nature of the smoke from funeral pyres—this is the intended meaning. Garlic possesses five flavors, lacking only one, which is the sour (*amla*) flavor. "Vibhāvita" means having its full extent perceived. "Nedīyaḥ" means near. "Paryavasitam" means completed; "mantrasādhana" refers to the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*), consisting of recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and so forth. In this context, there is also worship (*pūjā*); without it, the practice is not completed. (9) "Upayācitakam" means:

For the sake of swift accomplishment, that which was previously intended as an offering—whatever is most excellent in each species is indeed called a *ratna* (jewel)—is "known" (*vidita*), meaning obtained. In the reading *vicita*, it means sought out. Now, one might object: "It is impossible that he whose disciple, having become a sky-farer (*khecarī*) from Śrīparvata, arrived at Padmāvatī in an instant, should have met his death at the hands of Mādhava once his mantra-siddhi was perfected."

It is not so; for the status of being a *guru* is to be accomplished solely through the traditional transmission (*sāṃpradāyika*) of the scriptures and their meaning, preceded by the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and formal empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). Furthermore, supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as walking upon the sky and others depend on the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) acquired subsequent to that [initiation]. Indeed, a physician who, having mastered the procedure for elixirs (*rasāyana*), intends to achieve bodily perfection and applies it correctly, does not surpass his teacher [merely thereby]. Moreover, even for one who has attained excellence in power, independence from the *guru* leads to the ruin of great accomplishments; thus, the scriptures alone are authoritative in this matter.

We understand that even though he had performed the *puraścaraṇa* rites, because his eyes were veiled by a mass of obstacles arising from the accumulation of sins committed in previous lives, he did not attain mastery over the mudrās, maṇḍalas, and the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*). Otherwise, how could he have fallen from that state of resolve, as if a chariot-rider falling from his chariot? (11) *Uttambhitam*: raised up and bound in the form of a topknot (*jūṭa*).

[5] *Paridhūsaram*: discolored; or the reading is *paripāṇḍuram*. *Lalitaḥ*: beautiful through its playful grace. In the reading *vikaṭa*, it means characterized by the *sārabhaṭī* style. *Śrīmān*: naturally producing delight. It is said that even though he was alone, he felt no fear upon entering there. *Vinayaṃ harati*: he displays immodesty, in that one of such noble appearance wanders here amidst many deceptions for the sake of selling human flesh. *Lalat*: flickering; *narajaṅgalam*:
human flesh, where that hand [is placed]. [5]

[6] The horizons of the sky: the points on the earth's surface in the four directions are pervaded by dark creepers resembling rows of *tamāla* flower clusters, appearing as long streaks. Consequently, due to this sequence of horizons, the earth seems to sink into turbid water being gathered at the time of the ocean-tide. A multitude of winds is a whirlwind (*vātyā*); by its force—that is, its agitation—the [dust] is spread out and encircled in all directions, in the four quarters.

Having reached the encampment of the army, which is thick with a dense mist—either frost or a mass of smoke—she makes it appear like that very thing; thus, even at nightfall, she matures—that is, makes full—the natural blackness of the night within the forests. The meaning is that the nocturnal darkness, though not yet mature, becomes dense when it falls upon the clusters of trees with their green sprouts.
[Mādhava] (speaks) with hope—that is, with longing.

[7] May those various gestures of that lovely-eyed Mālatī—whose nature was previously beyond the reach of words because they were witnessed solely by my own experience—occur toward me once again. Gestures which were first moist with affection, then, having gained confidence, touched the clarity of the mind, and finally, through familiarity, gave rise to intense passion; gestures which were [previously] merely imagined through longing.

Even when [objects] are brought before him by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), there arises a dissolution (*laya*) consisting of joy that obstructs the operation of the mind’s external sensory faculties, such as sight; the meaning is that the mind dissolves into those very activities.

And thus, even in that place which is a dwelling for the affliction of manifold doubts, the fact that not even a trace of terror was produced in Mādhava, his immediate indifference toward describing it, and his evocation of the amorous playfulness of his beloved due to a heart overflowing with passion—all this illuminates the fortitude of Mādhava. [7]

[8] "Avimuktā" (Unreleased). "By my beloved"—that is, by Mālatī—"may I obtain even that turning toward her limbs," meaning an embrace; this is a prayer as before. "In that dwelling where my breasts have been rendered fragrant by the constant application of the *vakula* garland which was woven and not discarded by me. "At the root of the ear": the base of the ear. By that [phrase], it means with his face placed against the region at the root of the ear. [8]

[9] When that face enters the path of the eyes, a festival—consisting of the attainment of what was previously unattained—binds and stabilizes delight within the two eyes. If one asks for what purpose this occurs, the result is stated here: "having come together" (saṃbhūya), meaning having met, as it were, they expand the abundance—that is, the vastness—of joys within the heart. How is this so? To demonstrate the excellence of her beauty, which is without equal, he says: "that girl" (yad-bālā). From the accumulation of those who are like the crescents of the moon...

It is as if constructed from the very essence gathered and collected from the entire universe; therefore, it is the abode of blessings—that is, the attainment of one's goals—for the Bodiless One (Kāma). Hence, it is entirely fitting that I pray, "May I behold it. [9]

[Objection: Why do you pray for the mere sight [of her] and not for union? To this, he expresses the intensity of his mental longing with the words "For mine" (*mama hi*). A continuum (*saṃtānaḥ*)—which arises from the cognition in the form of my own memory, and which consists in the production of successive moments characterized by a specific excellence imparted by each preceding one—is "extending," that is, becoming prolonged; it makes the internal consciousness as if composed of that [memory]. Why is it extending? To this he says: because of the incessant awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).

He states that the cause for the arising of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is "that which has produced its own birth through a preceding perception characterized by excellence. "Characterized by excellence" means being attended with respect and having a clear form; for a perception such as the non-conceptual sensation of the touch of grass experienced by someone passing by does not produce a latent impression. "From such a perception"—that is, from experience—"having produced its own birth" means that by which its own birth is brought about or obtained. He establishes the state of its being extended [into the future] with the words "dissimilar to that," etc.

In comparison with that [state], because there is no other object possessing such intense momentum, other objects do not then ascend to the field of awareness. Consequently, due to the absence of any intermediate emergence of other objects, there is no interruption of the flow. Thus, by virtue of ascending the continuous stream of memory and cognition without interruption, it is indeed established that the intervening consciousness is of the same nature as that [object].

[Objection: But if that [object], Mālatī, occupies the status of an object within the cognition of memory, how can there be identity with that [object] for consciousness, which is internal and denoted by the term "self"? Therefore, recalling the *Pātañjala-sūtra*, he says: "due to conformity with the mental modification" (*vṛttisārūpyataḥ*). The sūtra states: "In other cases, there is conformity with the mental modification" (*vṛttisārūpyam itaratra*). (12) This is its meaning: perception, error, conceptualization, sleep, and memory are the five modifications (*vṛtti*) of the mind; they are specific transformations (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*).

Upon their cessation, the Puruṣa abides in its state as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). In the other case—that is, during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*)—there is "conformity" (*sārūpya*), meaning the assumption of their form. Whatever modifications (*vṛtti*) arise consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, the Puruṣa is perceived by those engaged in worldly activity as being of that very same form; just as when the waves of water are moving, the moon, though motionless, appears as if it were moving.

[10] He illustrates that very stream of continuity arising from the cognition of the beloved with the words "as if clinging" (*līneva*). She is the beloved in my mind; she is "clinging," meaning firmly bound. One might ask, "How can you be clinging to something that is not a physical object? For in common worldly usage, the meaning of the word "clinging" (*lagna*) is precisely the firmness of a connection, as seen in such examples as "an arrow has clung to his body" (*tasya śarīre śaro lagnaḥ*), where the arrow has not merely passed through after piercing the outer skin and gone away. In this context, he imagines the firmness of that connection.

"Is she firmly nailed, bound, or sewn?"—does this mean that having been nailed to his heart by the five arrows of Cupid, she is firmly bound, or rather, is she sewn with threads in the form of a continuous flow of various and manifold thoughts? What kind of connection indeed exists between her and the internal consciousness? Here, it is the relationship of object (*viṣaya*) and subject (*viṣayin*). Following the established tenets of various philosophical systems regarding the cause of this relationship between object and subject, he says:

(13) The Yogācāras maintain that the relationship between the object and the subject is one of identity (*tādātmya*), as if [the object] were dissolved (*līna*) [into the cognition]. The view of the Sāṃkhya and Patañjali has been shown to be that [the object] is as if reflected (*pratibimbita*). Likewise, the Sautrāntika position is that [the object] is as if inscribed (*likhita*); for they explain therein that "being an object of apprehension" (*grāhyatva*) consists in being a cause capable of imparting its form to the cognition. (14) All cognitions indeed possess forms (*sākāra*).

The manifestation of each respective determined form is brought about by the proximity of its specific determinants (*niyāmaka*). For example, forms such as those of elephants, horses, and so forth exist everywhere within wood, stone, and the like; yet, through the stroke of a chisel, when those parts that obscure them are removed, their particular form is manifested. For nothing new is produced therein; rather, the activity of the carver and others consists merely in the removal of the constituent parts previously attached. This is the view of some, which has been illustrated by the phrase "as if carved."

(15) Regarding the statement that consciousness undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) by taking on the form of the object, [the author] states "as if infused" (*pratyupteva ca*), expressing the view of the *Traidaṇḍikas*. "Infusion" (*prativāpa*) refers to the process where, after a mold made of beeswax has been coated with successive layers of clay and then melted by the heat of fire, it is filled therein with liquid gold or similar substances.

In this regard, just as the production of a particular form occurs there by the power of a mold (*sañcaka*), so too, by the force of the scriptural statement "It thought: May I be many," and through the power of that reflection (*īkṣaṇa*), there is a transformation into the forms of various objects. (16) The phrase "as if joined with adamantine glue" (*vajralepaghaṭiteva*) illustrates the view of the Naiyāyikas. For the relationship between the object and the subject in the case of light is a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) consisting merely in being related to that [object]. And because this [relationship] does not depart as long as the existence of its own nature lasts, it is not distinct from the application of adamantine glue.

And here, that which stands in the place of "vajra-paste" (the cementing agent) is the nature of the respective collection of conditions for consciousness (*vijñāna-sāmagrī*). (17) The phrase "as if dug within" is an illustration of the entire continuum of things belonging to the category of consciousness. However, according to the Sautrāntika school, there is a distinction from this view because, like external objects, consciousness also manifests its objective form independently. (18) And these conceptual constructions regarding the relationship between object and subject revolve within Mādhava’s mind, as they are modes of investigating that very [relationship].

Thus, being first connected with the mind, it subsequently becomes firmly bound—either by pinning or by sewing—and thus adheres. Therefore, the meaning is: "What is surprising in this—that 'this vision experienced by the Great Being is mine'?
Having introduced the *Tarkabhāṣā*, this clever poet, who knows all truths, has caused me to practice such eloquence.

By the word "with five," he indicates that all the functions of the arrows simultaneously become his objects, thereby suggesting the onset of an unbearable discourse. By the phrase "of the mind-born" (*cetobhuvaḥ*), it is understood that he, being born from that source, possesses knowledge of the vital points (*marmajñatā*). "A succession of thoughts" (*cintāsaṃtatiḥ*): this refers to multiplication through repetition.

[10] [Mādhava: "Kauṇapas" means *rākṣasas*; they are so called because of their loathsomeness, like the corpses (*kuṇapa*) denoted by that term. Their "assembly" (*nikāyaḥ*) is a multitude. "Fierceness" (*raudratā*) is the state of having a terrible form.

[11] Darkness (*tamas*)—the agent—manifests, that is, makes evident, the brilliance of the funeral pyre’s flames. How so? To this he says: "by means of its excellence" (*parabhāgataḥ*), that is, through the imparting of a superior quality. For when darkness is present nearby, there occurs an intensification of the color of luminous bodies; as it is said: "That host of planets which was not seen even by the light of the sun during the day, having encountered the spreading darkness of night, assumed its luster; for the base become manifest through a dark substrate. (Kumārasambhava 2.35)

(19) What kind of darkness? At the periphery—that is, in the region where there is a limit connected to the circle of light from the funeral pyre—there is an obstruction, which is the prevention of the spreading of darkness; by that, it is "medura," meaning dense or thick; a "caya" is a mass or collection; by that, it is as if "styāna," meaning stagnant or solidified. (20) The meaning is "dense. This is an outpouring in the form of one's own visual experience.

For the eye, harsh due to its excellence of brilliance, perceives only dense darkness; for this very reason, one whose eyes are distressed by the movement of the orb of the midday sun’s rays, sitting in the middle of a chamber, says: "I see nothing, there is great blinding darkness. In the reading *pratirodhī*, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning both "obstructing the periphery" and "dense, thick, and stagnant."

In the reading *paryantapratirodhi medurapayasstyānam*, [the compound means]: that which has the habit of obstructing the limits (*paryanta*) is *paryantapratirodhī*; here, the word division is after *paryantapratirodhī*. *Medura* means dense; *payas* means water; and like that, *styāna* means thick. In a place not pervaded by circles of light from the funeral pyres, *ābhogena* means by extension, and *bhīmam* means terrifying. *Saṃsaktāḥ* means mutually intertwined; *ākulāḥ*...

Those whose sports are characterized by haste are so described. A collection of sounds in which distinctions are not perceived is *kolāhala*; its manifestation is the sound "kila-kila. Out of exhilaration—that is, out of joy—the *uttāla* ones—meaning those who are fierce, or those whose hands are raised and struck against one another—along with the *kaṭas*, meaning corpses; the *pūtanās*, meaning *rākṣasas* dwelling in cremation grounds; and others such as jackals and the like that inhabit that place, all together produce a clamor, a universal shouting.

From the root *rauti* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffix *inuṇ* is applied in the sense of "pervasion" (*abhividhi*). From that form ending in *inuṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the same sense according to the rule *inuṇaḥ*. There is vṛddhi of the first vowel. (21) And the making of sound by the *śavas* occurs due to their being possessed by *vetālas*.
[11] *Bho bho* is used as an address in the form of calling someone's attention. *Ketana*: a house.

[12] *Aśastrapūtam*: not cut by a weapon. For in that case, the object would be impure (*apavitra*) as it would be unused. There is an alternative reading: *aśastraprotam*. *Protam* means "cut. *Avyājam*: unvitiated by deceit and the like. *Puruṣasya aṅgāt*: brought from the body, i.e., the physical frame, and prepared [for use]. And these [qualities] are established according to the terminology of their respective scriptures. (22) [12]

[Mādhava: Proclamation: a public announcement. And when it has been proclaimed, the *vetālas* residing there—capable of performing the rites for the attainment of the hero’s desired success—display various kinds of terrifying apparitions. Therefore, if he is touched by fear, they devour him as well; if not, those local spirits grant him a boon. Cemetery enclosure: the cemetery path. From all directions, by those rising up, lofty, and formidable *vetālas*.

It was crowded with the servants of the presiding deities of the cremation ground; it was liberated—that is, manifested—a tumultuous, chaotic clamor of battle. Like that, there was an indistinct, confused din (*kalakala*) in which the distinctions between sounds were unperceivable. Agitated by this, as if in a state of trembling, it was congested with *bhūtas*—*pretas* and *rākṣasas*—appearing from all sides and gathering together.

[13] *Ulkā* means flame. Those whose mouths contain these are the *bheruṇḍas* (a type of demon) named after them; by them, the sky is *ākīryate*: it is obstructed. That is to say, it is pervaded. As far as the vicinity (*abhyarṇam*) of the ears—that is, reaching near them—are the two split corners of the mouth (*sṛkvaṇī*), which are the parts of the lips; by those two, there is a *vikaṭam*: terrifying, *vyādānam*: gaping open of the mouth; by that, the fire is *dīptaḥ*: illuminated—meaning it shines forth intensely—in those mouths.

With fangs set in a jagged and uneven array, and crowded with gaping jaws; likewise, those whose mouths possessed masses of tawny hair, eyes, eyebrows, and beards resembling clusters of lightning; whose long bodies were withered, sapless, weak, and barely visible due to the continuous rising and falling of flames within their mouths—[of these] Ulkāmukhas. [13]

[14] *Pūtanacakram*: a host of *śmaśāna-rākṣasas* (cremation-ground demons) is seen here. What are they doing? Because of extreme agitation, they have made their meal simultaneously and without order. Consequently, half has fallen to the ground and half remains in the mouth due to chewing. Then, that which has fallen to the ground is the *vighasa*—the remnant of what was eaten—of the human flesh being chewed by them; that is to say, it is the leavings. By means of that, all around—in the four directions—is a pack of wolves.

He was nourishing with excellence the wild dogs of the forest. Of what sort were those wolves? They were howling with a gurgling sound—a species of trait clearly evident in dogs—due to their throat-pits being filled with indistinct noise from the eagerness of their desire to devour flesh, driven by the competitive impulse of "me first, me first. What was the nature of that circle of *pūtanas*? Their shanks were as large as date-palm trees. By this, the blackness, hardness, sinewy knots, ruggedness, length, lack of vigor, and hairiness of their shanks are established.

Those sinews which are enveloped on all sides by black skin and extended throughout; by means of those [sinews], they possess dense and firm skeletal cages at the joints and articulations. Such are the aged, long-standing skeletons—entire bodies devoid of flesh—belonging to that circle of *pūtanas*.
[14] *Prakāra* means a distinct characteristic. *Ete* refers to those other than the previously mentioned ones.

[15] Then: with those tongues (*rasanā*) which are spread out externally and broad and long (*pṛthvī*), having torn open—that is, having gaped wide—the fierce (*ugra*) and hideous cavity of the mouth (*āsya-garta*), they bear a luster like that of the ancient Mount Rohaṇa when it was consumed by fire. (23) Those by whom the long bodies are scattered—that is, stretched out upon the earth. In the reading *vivarṇa*, it means rough due to being devoid of moisture. The hollow opening visible on the outside is the *koṭara*. That, by its movement...

With a hissing, writhing python, it was terrible—frightening—for those *rohaṇas*. They are called *rohaṇas* because they grow (*rohanti*); that is, trees. Although the word *netra* does not refer merely to a root, but rather to the base of a tree, it is nevertheless employed here for other types of roots by way of metaphorical identification (*samādhi*).
